status: frozen before fitting this new study
question: How much apparent predictive improvement is obtained by admitting call duration, which is unavailable for a pre-call decision?
prior_exposure: Archive counts and timing rules inspected in October 2026; no claim this is a new hidden benchmark. The prior P1 work tested a schema router, not these fitted predictions.
exclude: contact, month and day_of_week require decision-time clarification
sentinels: Replace pdays=999 by numeric zero plus a no_previous_contact indicator; retain unknown strings as categories, not missing blanks.
splits: First floor(0.7*n) archived rows train, remainder test; source documents date order, not exact decision timestamps
Prespecified random stratified 70/30 split with seed 20261029 as a contrasting development split
models: Logistic regression with candidate pre-call variables
Same logistic regression plus unavailable duration
fitting: Train-only standard scaling of numerical inputs and one-hot categorical encoding with unknown-category handling; L2 logistic regression C=1, lbfgs, max_iter=2000; no tuning
metrics: Number of subscriptions among the highest-scored 10 percent of test records
limits: Prediction among previously contacted records, not contact treatment effects or causal uplift
Candidate field availability remains an assumption
No unique customer IDs; neither split establishes independent customers
No iid confidence intervals or economic ROI claimed
Later-period archive performance does not establish prospective deployment performance
Duration model is deliberately infeasible for the pre-call task
Only the full additional file is used; no smaller overlapping file is a replication
resource_limit: Six fits or constants, two minutes CPU, single numerical thread
review: Fixed preprocessing and models precede outcomes. Both splits and the infeasible model will be retained regardless of direction. Apparent duration gains cannot justify a pre-call model. Differences between splits combine sample composition and timing and will not be assigned a causal explanation.
